title: Account bucketization and runway credits for escalated feature requests
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Design and ship a structured mechanism that turns high-touch account escalations into quantified roadmap commitments using a lightweight bucketization model and transferable 'runway credits'. The goal is to reduce ad-hoc promises, improve predictability for engineering capacity planning, and provide a measurable SLA for top accounts that request expedited feature work.
background: We regularly receive escalations from strategic customers asking for priority delivery of features. Engineering and GTM teams often make informal verbal commitments which are hard to track and create scope churn. Current intake suffers from two problems: (1) Lack of a canonical exposure of how many escalations can be accepted in a quarter, and (2) No standardized composable response that preserves fairness across accounts while enabling rapid action when necessary.
proposal: Introduce an 'Account Buckets' model (Gold/Silver/Bronze) and a quarterly runway credit pool. Each qualifying escalation consumes runway credits based on expected engineering effort and risk. Credits can be allocated from: (a) a reserved enterprise fastpass pool, (b) negotiated conversion of existing priority credits, or (c) paid acceleration credits (for customers on dedicated plans). The feature will include: intake form extensions, a deterministic credit calculator, automated ledgering in the intake dashboard, and an SLA page exposed to account teams.
acceptance_criteria: Intake form includes estimated credit cost and business justification
Automated ledger records assigned credits and current balance per account
Dashboard shows projected runway consumption for next 90 days
Policy enforces maximum per-account quarterly credit spend
At least 2 pilot accounts complete 1 simulated escalation flow
Engineering and Sales sign-off on credit costing model
tradeoffs: Pros: predictable capacity planning, fewer verbal commitments, measurable fairness
Cons: increases administrative overhead for small escalations, potential for customers to game estimates
We may need to reserve capacity that could lower total throughput if utilization is low
